summary: Gives guidelines for designing congestion notification in lower-layer or tunnelling protocols that encapsulate IP. The aim is for explicit congestion signals to travel consistently into IP and up to the transport layer. It is a Best Current Practice and updates RFC 3819.

plainLanguage.summary: When a queue in a router fills up, the router can either drop a packet or mark it to say the network is busy. Marking is better, because the sender can then slow down before anything is lost. This document says how a protocol that sits below IP, such as a tunnel or an Ethernet link, should carry that mark so that IP can pass it on. It describes four possible behaviours and the rules to follow at each end of a tunnel.

questions: how to add ecn to a tunnel protocol
how should a tunnel egress handle ecn marks
subtitle: How a protocol below IP, such as a tunnel or an Ethernet link, should carry a congestion marking up to IP.

tldr.problem: Explicit Congestion Notification lets a router mark a packet instead of dropping it, but the mark only works if every layer below IP that carries it passes it on. Most tunnel and subnet protocols have no defined way to do that.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC divides lower-layer behaviour into four modes and gives rules for each: a lower layer must not mark packets whose receiver cannot understand the mark or whose egress would swallow it, the ingress must confirm the egress propagates the mark, and the egress must calculate the outgoing field from both the inner and outer headers.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is included in BCP 89 and updates the ECN advice in RFC 3819, so that ECN support can be added consistently to tunnelling protocols and subnet technologies.

today: RFC 9599 is a Best Current Practice published in August 2024 and included in BCP 89. It updates RFC 3819 by replacing the ECN advice in Section 13 of that document with a reference to this one, and no later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Congestion Marks Have to Cross Layers
sections.content:
In certain networks it is possible for traffic to congest nodes that are not aware of IP. The benefits of Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) can only be fully realized if support for congestion notification is added to the relevant subnetwork technology as well as to IP. When a lower-layer buffer implicitly notifies congestion by dropping a packet, it does not just drop at that layer: the packet disappears from all layers. In contrast, when active queue management (AQM) at a lower layer buffer explicitly notifies congestion by marking a frame header, the marking has to be propagated up the layers explicitly. The same is true if the AQM marks the outer header of a packet that encapsulates inner tunnelled headers. Forwarding ECN is not as straightforward as other headers, because it has to be assumed that ECN may be only partially deployed: if a lower-layer header that contains congestion indications is stripped off by a subnet egress that is not ECN-aware, or if the ultimate receiver or sender is not ECN-aware, congestion has to be indicated by dropping the packet, not marking it.

ECN is defined in the IP header, for IPv4 and IPv6, to allow a resource to notify the onset of queue buildup without having to drop packets, by explicitly marking a proportion of packets with the congestion experienced (CE) codepoint. Given a suitable marking scheme, ECN removes nearly all congestion loss and cuts delays for two main reasons. It avoids the delay when recovering from congestion losses, which particularly benefits small flows or real-time flows, making their delivery time predictably short. And as ECN is used more widely by end systems, it gradually removes the need to configure a degree of delay into buffers before they start to notify congestion, which is the cause of bufferbloat, because drop involves a trade-off between sending a timely signal and trying to avoid impairment, whereas ECN is solely a signal and not an impairment.

Some lower-layer technologies, such as MPLS and Ethernet, are used to form subnetworks with IP-aware nodes only at the edges. Propagation of ECN is defined for MPLS and for TRILL, but it has yet to be defined for a number of other subnetwork technologies. Similarly, ECN propagation is yet to be defined for many tunnelling protocols: RFC 6040 defines how ECN should be propagated for IP-in-IPv4, IP-in-IPv6 and IPsec tunnels, but there are numerous other tunnelling protocols with a shim and/or a Layer 2 header between two IP headers. Some address ECN propagation between the IP headers, but many do not.

Incremental deployment is the most delicate aspect when adding support for ECN. The original ECN protocol in IP was carefully designed so that a congested buffer would not mark a packet, rather than drop it, unless both source and destination hosts were ECN-capable. To support congestion marking below the IP layer or within tunnels, it is not sufficient to check only that the two layer 4 transport endpoints support ECN. Correct operation also depends on the decapsulator at each subnet or tunnel egress faithfully propagating congestion notification to the higher layer. Otherwise a legacy decapsulator might silently fail to propagate any congestion signals from the outer header to the forwarded header, and the lost signals would never be detected, so congestion would build up further.

The IETF does not have standards authority over every link-layer protocol, so this document gives guidelines for designing propagation of congestion notification across the interface between IP and protocols that may encapsulate IP. Each lower-layer technology will exhibit different issues and compromises, so the capitalized terms SHOULD and SHOULD NOT are often used in preference to MUST or MUST NOT. If a particular protocol design chooses not to follow a SHOULD or SHOULD NOT given in the advice, it MUST include a sound justification.

The document also updates the brief advice to subnetwork designers about ECN in Section 13 of RFC 3819, replacing the last two paragraphs with a reference to this document. Its scope is wire protocol processing of explicit notification of congestion; it makes no changes or recommendations concerning algorithms for congestion marking or congestion response, because those algorithm issues should be independent of the layer the algorithm operates in. It focuses on the interface between IP and lower-layer or tunnel protocols, where IP includes IPv4 or IPv6, unicast, multicast or anycast. The guidelines do not necessarily require the subnet wire protocol to be changed: the feed-up-and-forward mode and the null mode do not. In the feed-backward mode, propagation of congestion signals for multicast and anycast packets is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A congestion mark is only useful if every device on the path keeps it. If a tunnel or a link layer drops the mark, the sender never learns that the network is busy. This document gives the rules that keep the mark intact as it travels up through the layers.

sections.title: The Terms Used
sections.content:
The document defines the vocabulary it uses:

  • A protocol data unit (PDU) is information delivered as a unit among peer entities of a layered network, consisting of protocol control information, typically a header, and possibly user data. In Layer 2 and Layer 3 networks the PDU is respectively termed a frame or a packet, or a cell in ATM.
  • Transport means the end-to-end transmission control function, conventionally at layer 4 in the OSI reference model. The document qualifies it as L4 transport where the audience would otherwise read it as low-level bit carriage.
  • The encapsulator is the link or tunnel endpoint function that adds an outer header to a PDU, also termed the link ingress or the ingress tunnel endpoint. The decapsulator removes an outer header from a PDU, also termed the link egress or the egress tunnel endpoint.
  • The incoming header is the header of an arriving PDU before encapsulation. The outer header is the header added to encapsulate a PDU, the inner header is the header the outer header encapsulates, and the outgoing header is the header forwarded by the decapsulator.
  • CE is Congestion Experienced, ECT is ECN-Capable (L4) Transport, and Not-ECT is Not ECN-Capable (L4) Transport.
  • The Load Regulator is, for each flow of PDUs, the transport function that is capable of controlling the data rate. It is typically located at the data source, but in-path nodes can regulate load in some congestion control arrangements, such as admission control, policing nodes or transport circuit-breakers.
  • An ECN-PDU is a PDU at the IP layer or below with a capacity to signal congestion, that is part of a congestion control feedback loop within which all the nodes necessary to propagate the signal back to the Load Regulator are capable of doing that propagation. An IP packet with a non-zero ECN field implies that the endpoints are ECN-capable. A Not-ECN-PDU is a PDU at the IP layer or below that is part of a feedback loop that cannot propagate ECN signals back to the Load Regulator, because at least one of the nodes needed to do so is incapable of it. This is a property of the feedback loop, not necessarily of the PDU itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The document names the two ends of a tunnel: the encapsulator adds the outer header and the decapsulator removes it. It also names the two kinds of packet: one on a path where every device can carry a congestion signal back to the sender, and one where they cannot.

sections.title: Four Modes of Operation
sections.content:
The document sets down four modes by which congestion information is passed between the lower layer and the higher one, as a reference framework for the guidelines that follow.

  • Feed-Forward-and-Up: nodes feed forward congestion notification towards the egress within the lower layer, then up and along the layers towards the end-to-end destination at the transport layer. Many subnet technologies, like IP and MPLS, are based on self-contained PDUs or frames sent unreliably and provide no feedback channel at the subnetwork layer, relying on higher layers such as TCP to feed back loss signals. For them, ECN is best supported by standardising explicit notification of congestion into the lower-layer protocol that carries the data forwards, with a specification for how the egress of the lower-layer subnet propagates the explicit signal into the forwarded upper-layer IP header. The signal continues forwards until it reaches the destination transport, which typically feeds the notification back to the source transport using an end-to-end protocol such as TCP. This is the arrangement already used to add ECN to IP-in-IP tunnels, IP-in-MPLS and MPLS-in-MPLS.
  • Feed-Up-and-Forward: a lower-layer switch feeds up congestion notification directly into the higher layer, for example into the ECN field in the IP header, irrespective of whether the node is at the egress of a subnet. Ethernet is particularly difficult to extend incrementally in this way, because it is usually done with so-called Layer 3 switches, which dig into the Ethernet payload to find an IP header and manipulate or act on certain IP fields, specifically Diffserv and ECN. With respect to switching, a Layer 3 switch acts solely on the addresses in the Ethernet header; it does not use IP addresses and it does not decrement the TTL field in the IP header.
  • Feed-Backward: nodes feed back congestion signals towards the ingress of the lower layer and, optionally, attempt to control congestion within their own layer. The relative rate mechanism for the Available Bit Rate service in ATM is an example: ATM switches send special resource management cells in both the forward and backward directions to control the ingress rate of user data into a virtual circuit, and if a switch buffer is approaching congestion or is congested, it sends a resource management cell back towards the ingress with the No Increase or Congestion Indication bit set, so the ingress holds or decreases its sending bit rate.
  • Null: nodes cannot experience congestion at the lower layer except at the ingress nodes of the subnet, which are IP-aware or equivalently higher-layer-aware. Link- and physical-layer resources are often non-blocking by design. A degenerate example is a point-to-point Ethernet link, where excess loading merely causes the queue from the higher layer to back up while the lower layer remains immune to congestion.

The Forward Explicit Congestion Notification bit in Frame Relay and the Explicit Forward Congestion Indication bit in ATM user data cells follow a feed-forward pattern, but in ATM this was only part of a feed-forward-and-backward pattern at the lower layer, and the intention was never to interface with IP-ECN at the subnet egress.
sections.plainLanguage: Lower layers pass congestion information in one of four ways. They can mark packets as they travel forward and copy the mark upwards when a header is removed, mark the IP header directly, send a message backwards to the sender of the traffic, or never congest at all. The guidelines follow these four cases.

sections.title: What a Lower Layer May Mark
sections.content:
The guidelines for the design of a lower-layer congestion notification system are these:

  • It SHOULD NOT apply explicit congestion notifications to PDUs that are destined for legacy layer 4 transport implementations that will not understand ECN.
  • It SHOULD NOT apply explicit congestion notifications to PDUs if the egress of the subnet might not propagate congestion notification onward into the higher layer.
  • It SHOULD be able to distinguish ECN-PDUs from Not-ECN-PDUs.

A PDU on a feedback loop that meets both of the first two criteria is called an ECN-PDU, because it will propagate congestion notification properly. A PDU on a feedback loop that does not meet at least one of the criteria is a Not-ECN-PDU and will not.

There is no need for all interior nodes within a subnet to be able to mark congestion explicitly; a mix of drop and explicit congestion signals from different nodes is fine. However, if any interior nodes might generate congestion markings, all relevant egress nodes SHOULD be able to propagate those markings up to the higher layer.

In IP, if the ECN field in each PDU is cleared to the Not ECN-Capable Transport codepoint, it indicates that the L4 transport will not understand congestion markings, and a congested buffer must not mark such PDUs, so it has to signal congestion by increasingly applying drop instead. The mechanism a lower layer uses to distinguish the ECN capability of PDUs need not mimic that of IP; the guidelines merely say that the lower-layer system as a whole should achieve the same outcome. ECN-capable feedback loops might use PDUs identified by a particular set of labels or tags, logical-link protocols that use flow state might determine whether a PDU can be congestion marked by checking for ECN support in the flow state, and other protocols might depend on out-of-band control signals.

The per-domain checking of ECN support in MPLS is a good example of a way to avoid sending congestion markings to L4 transports that will not understand them, without using any header space in the subnet protocol. In MPLS, header space is extremely limited, so no field in the MPLS header indicates whether the PDU is an ECN-PDU. Instead, interior nodes in a domain are allowed to set explicit congestion indications without checking the PDU's destination, and this is made safe by requiring the network operator to upgrade all decapsulating edges of a whole domain at once, as soon as even one switch within the domain is configured to mark rather than drop. When decapsulating a CE-marked packet, if the decapsulator discovers that the higher layer indicates the transport is not ECN-capable, it drops the packet, effectively on behalf of the earlier congested node.

That incremental deployment strategy was only appropriate for MPLS, which is targeted at professional operators who can be expected to ensure that a whole subnetwork is consistently configured. It might not be appropriate for link technologies targeted at zero-configuration deployment or deployment by the general public, such as Ethernet, where a fail-safe approach is needed so that congestion markings never fall into black holes no matter how inconsistently a system is put together. ECN support in TRILL provides an example of such an approach: TRILL provides an extension header word with space for flags of different categories, and the congestion-experienced marking is defined as a critical ingress-to-egress flag. If a transit RBridge sets this flag on a frame and an egress RBridge has no logic to process it, the egress RBridge drops the frame, which is the desired default action anyway. TRILL RBridges can therefore be updated with support for congestion notification in no particular order.
sections.plainLanguage: A lower layer may only mark a packet when two things hold: the transport at the far end understands the mark, and the far end of the subnet will pass it on. The protocol has to be able to tell those packets apart from the rest, and it must fail safely if some device in the path does not understand the mark.

sections.title: Guidelines at the Ingress
sections.content:
The guidelines for the redesign of a node that encapsulates IP with a lower-layer header are these.

  • Egress Capability Check. A subnet ingress needs to be sure that the corresponding egress of the subnet will propagate any congestion notification added to the outer header across the subnet. This is necessary in addition to checking that an incoming PDU indicates an ECN-capable transport. Examples of how this guarantee might be provided are by configuration, as in MPLS, where if any label switch in a domain supports congestion marking, all egress nodes are required to have been configured to propagate ECN; by the ingress explicitly checking that the egress propagates ECN, as in an early attempt to add ECN support to TRILL, which used IS-IS to check path capabilities before adding ECN extension flags to each frame; and by inherent design of the protocol, by encoding the congestion marking on the outer header in such a way that a legacy egress that does not understand ECN will consider the PDU corrupt or invalid and discard it, so at least a form of congestion signal is propagated.
  • Egress Fails Capability Check. If the ingress cannot guarantee that the egress will propagate congestion notification, the ingress SHOULD disable congestion notification at the lower layer when it forwards the PDU. One way to do that is by setting the outer header of the PDU to identify it as a Not-ECN-PDU, assuming the subnet technology supports such a concept.
  • Standard Congestion Monitoring Baseline. Once the ingress to a subnet has established that the egress will correctly propagate ECN, it SHOULD encode the same level of congestion in outer headers as is arriving in incoming headers, for example by copying any incoming congestion notifications into the outer header of the lower-layer protocol. This ensures that bulk congestion monitoring of outer headers measures congestion accumulated along the whole upstream path, starting from the Load Regulator and not just from the ingress of the subnet. A node that is not the Load Regulator SHOULD NOT re-initialize the level of CE markings in the outer header to zero.

It is still possible to measure the congestion introduced across one subnet or tunnel by subtracting the level of CE markings on inner headers from that on outer headers. For example, if the guideline has been followed and the level of CE markings is 0.4 percent on the outer header and 0.1 percent on the inner header, 0.4 percent congestion has been introduced across all the networks since the Load Regulator, and 0.3 percent has been introduced since the ingress to the current subnet. Without the guideline, if the subnet ingress had re-initialized the outer congestion level to zero, the outer and inner headers would measure 0.1 percent and 0.3 percent, and the congestion introduced since the Load Regulator could only be inferred as 0.4 percent if the monitoring system somehow knew whether the ingress re-initialized the level. As long as subnet and tunnel technologies use the standard congestion monitoring baseline, monitoring systems know to use the former approach.
sections.plainLanguage: At the near end of a tunnel, the device first checks that the far end will pass a congestion mark on. If it cannot be sure, it must not mark packets at all. If it can be sure, it must copy the congestion level already seen into the outer header, so that monitoring measures the whole path rather than only the last hop.

sections.title: Guidelines at the Egress
sections.content:
A subnet egress SHOULD NOT simply copy congestion notifications from outer headers to the forwarded header. It SHOULD calculate the outgoing congestion notification field from the inner and outer headers using the following guidelines. If there is any conflict, rules earlier in the list take precedence over rules later in the list.

  • If the arriving inner header is a Not-ECN-PDU, it implies the L4 transport will not understand explicit congestion markings. If the outer header carries an explicit congestion marking, it is likely that a protocol error has occurred, so drop is the only indication of congestion that the L4 transport will understand. If the outer congestion marking is the most severe possible, the packet MUST be dropped. If congestion can be marked with multiple levels of severity and the packet's outer marking is not the most severe, this requirement is relaxed to: the packet SHOULD be dropped. If the outer is an ECN-PDU that carries no indication of congestion, or a Not-ECN-PDU, the PDU SHOULD be forwarded, but still as a Not-ECN-PDU.
  • If the outer header does not support congestion notification, a Not-ECN-PDU, but the inner header does, an ECN-PDU, the inner header SHOULD be forwarded unchanged.
  • In some lower-layer protocols, congestion may be signalled as a numerical level, such as in the control frames of QCN. If such a multi-bit encoding encapsulates an ECN-capable IP data packet, a function is needed to convert the quantized congestion level into the frequency of congestion markings in outgoing IP packets.
  • Congestion indications might be encoded by a severity level. For instance, increasing levels of congestion might be encoded by numerically increasing indications, as PCN can be encoded in each PDU at three severity levels in IP or MPLS. If the arriving inner header is an ECN-PDU where the inner and outer headers carry indications of congestion of different severity, the more severe indication SHOULD be forwarded in preference to the less severe.
  • The inner and outer headers might carry a combination of congestion notification fields that should not be possible given any currently used protocol transitions. If Encapsulation Guideline 3 had been followed, it should not be possible to have a less severe indication of congestion in the outer header than in the inner header. It MAY be appropriate to log unexpected combinations of headers and possibly raise an alarm. If a safe outgoing codepoint can be defined for such a PDU, the PDU SHOULD be forwarded rather than dropped. An approach using alarms and policy-mediated drop is preferable to hard-coded drop, so that operators can keep track of possible attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: At the far end of a tunnel, the device works out the outgoing congestion field from what the inner and outer headers say. If the transport inside cannot understand the mark, the packet is dropped instead, because a dropped packet is a signal that everyone understands.

sections.title: Feeding Up, and Feeding Back
sections.content:
Feed-up-and-forward is the mode that applies when IP packets are encapsulated in Ethernet headers, which have no support for congestion notification, or are forwarded by the base station of a 3GPP radio access network, which is required to apply ECN marking during congestion while the protocol that encapsulates the IP header over the radio access has no support for ECN. It generalizes to encapsulation by other subnet technologies with no built-in support for congestion notification at the lower layer, but with support for finding and processing an IP header. It is unlikely to be applicable or necessary for IP-in-IP encapsulation, where feed-forward-and-up mode based on RFC 6040 would be more appropriate.

Marking the IP header while switching at layer 2, by using a Layer 3 switch, or while forwarding in a radio access network seems to represent a layering violation. However, it can be considered a benign optimization if the guidelines are followed. It is certainly not a general alternative to implementing feed-forward congestion notification in the lower layer, because IPv4 and IPv6 are not the only Layer 3 protocols that might be encapsulated; link-layer encryption might be in use, making the Layer 2 payload inaccessible; many Ethernet switches do not have Layer 3 switch capabilities, so the ability to read or modify an IP payload cannot be assumed; and it might be costly to find an IP header when it may be encapsulated by more than one lower-layer header.

The guidelines are these. If a built-in lower-layer congestion notification mechanism exists for a subnet technology, it is safe to mix feed-up-and-forward with feed-forward-and-up on other switches in the same subnet, but it will generally be more efficient to use the built-in mechanism. The depth of the search for an IP header SHOULD be limited: if an IP header is not found soon enough, or an unrecognized or unreadable header is encountered, the switch SHOULD resort to an alternative means of signalling congestion, such as drop or the built-in lower-layer mechanism if available. It is sufficient to use the first IP header found in the stack, because the egress of the relevant tunnel can propagate congestion notification upwards to any more deeply encapsulated IP headers later.

For the feed-backward mode, the document says no detailed protocol design guidelines are appropriate, because the subnet tries to minimize congestion internally and, if the incoming load at the ingress exceeds the capacity somewhere through the subnet, the Layer 3 buffer into the ingress backs up. A feed-backward mode subnet is in some sense similar to a null mode subnet, in that there is no need for direct interaction between the subnet and higher-layer congestion notification. One general guideline does apply: a subnetwork technology intended to eventually interface to IP SHOULD NOT be designed using only the feed-backward mode, which is certainly best for a stand-alone subnet, but would need to be modified to work efficiently as part of the wider Internet because IP uses feed-forward-and-up mode.

Feed-backward can result in very inefficient and sluggish congestion control, except if it is confined to the subnet directly connected to the original data source when it is faster than feed-forward. It would be valid to design a protocol that works in feed-backward mode for paths that only cross one subnet, and in feed-forward-and-up mode for paths that cross subnets. In the early days of TCP/IP, a similar approach was tried for explicit congestion signalling using source-quench control packets, but that fell out of favour and is now formally deprecated. The main problem was that it is hard for a data source to tell the difference between a spoofed source-quench message and a quench request from a genuine buffer on the path, and it is also hard for a lower-layer buffer to address such a message to the original source port number, which may be buried within many layers of headers and possibly encrypted. QCN, also known as Backward Congestion Notification, uses a feed-backward mode that is structurally similar to the ATM relative rate mechanism, but confines its applicability to scenarios such as some data centres where all endpoints are directly attached by the same Ethernet technology. If a QCN subnet were later connected into a wider IP-based internetwork, it would suffer the inefficiency shown in the document's Figure 3.
sections.plainLanguage: Marking the IP header from a layer 2 switch is a shortcut that works only under stated limits, and the document sets them out. Sending congestion information backwards instead is deprecated for anything that will sit under IP, because the signal has to travel the wrong way and arrives too slowly.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
If a lower-layer wire protocol is redesigned to include explicit congestion signalling in-band in the protocol header, care SHOULD be taken to ensure that the field used is specified as mutable during transit. Otherwise, interior nodes signalling congestion would invalidate any authentication protocol applied to the lower-layer header, by altering a header field that had been assumed to be immutable.

The redesign of protocols that encapsulate IP in order to propagate congestion signals between layers raises potential signal integrity concerns. Experimental or proposed approaches exist for assuring the end-to-end integrity of in-band congestion signals, such as Congestion Exposure (ConEx) for networks, used to audit that their congestion signals are not being suppressed by other networks or by receivers, and to police that senders are responding sufficiently to the signals, irrespective of the L4 transport protocol used. Another is a test for a sender to detect whether a network or the receiver is suppressing congestion signals.

Given that these end-to-end approaches are already being specified, it would make little sense to attempt to design hop-by-hop congestion signal integrity into a new lower-layer protocol, because end-to-end integrity inherently achieves hop-by-hop integrity. The document also notes that Section 6 gives vulnerability to spoofing as one of the reasons for deprecating feed-backward mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things need care. A congestion field that interior nodes are allowed to change must not be covered by a checksum or signature that assumes it never changes. And because a mark that is removed along the path is invisible to the sender, the document points to end-to-end checks rather than per-hop protection.

The congested switch writes the mark straight into the IP header it finds in the payload
A control cell or frame is sent back towards the ingress, which slows down
The lower layer cannot congest, so only IP needs to signal

viz.caption: THE THREE RULES FOR WHAT A LOWER LAYER MAY MARK

items.title: Do not mark for legacy transports
items.text: The receiver's transport must understand ECN.

items.title: Do not mark if the egress will swallow it
items.text: The far end of the subnet must pass the mark upwards.

items.title: Tell the two kinds apart
items.text: The protocol must be able to recognise ECN-PDUs and Not-ECN-PDUs.

viz.caption: THE FIVE RULES AT THE EGRESS

items.title: 1. Inner header not ECN-capable
items.text: Drop the packet if the outer header carries a congestion marking.

items.title: 3. Numerical congestion level
items.text: Convert the level into a rate of congestion markings.

items.title: 5. Unexpected combination
items.text: Log it, raise an alarm, and forward if a safe codepoint exists.

viz.caption: THE RULES FOR FEEDING UP AND FORWARD

items.title: Mixing is safe
items.text: A built-in lower-layer mechanism can be used on other switches in the same subnet.

items.title: Limit the search depth
items.text: If no IP header is found soon, fall back to drop or the built-in mechanism.

items.title: The first IP header is enough
items.text: The tunnel egress can propagate the mark further up later.
